\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figs/fig1_dissociation.pdf}
\caption{(a) Counting accuracy against requested repetitions $k$. Every model
has a finite ceiling. (b) The same repeated items (solid) against their
length-matched controls (dashed), in which the repeated word is replaced by $k$
distinct fillers. Controls survive well past the point where repetitions fail:
the limit is on periodicity, not on length.}
\label{fig:dissociation}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{Counting collapses at a finite, model-specific $k^\ast$}

Figure~\ref{fig:dissociation}(a) shows counting accuracy against $k$ for all
\NModels{} checkpoints. Every model reproduces the qualitative shape the theorem
predicts: accuracy is high for small $k$, then falls to a floor and stays there.
Pooled over the panel, accuracy is \AccRepLow{}\% at $k\le3$ and
\AccRepHigh{}\% at $k\ge6$. Past the collapse point the errors are not random:
at $k\ge8$, \LoopPct{}\% of generations run long (looping or overcounting) and
\TruncPct{}\% stop short, which are precisely the two behaviours available to a
decoder whose stop decision has lost access to the count.

The collapse point $k^\ast$ ranges from \kStarMin{} to \kStarMax{} across the
panel (Table~\ref{tab:models}). It is not a simple function of parameter count:
the within-family Llasa ladder does not order $k^\ast$ monotonically with scale,
so whatever governs the horizon is not capacity.

\subsection{The limit is periodicity, not length}

Figure~\ref{fig:dissociation}(b) is the paper's sharpest test. Each control item
has the same carrier sentence and the same word count as its repeated twin, and
differs only in that the $k$ copies of one word are replaced by $k$ distinct
words. If the failure were about sequence length, attention span, or accumulated
exposure bias, the two curves would fall together. They do not: at $k\ge6$,
repeated items are rendered correctly \AccRepHigh{}\% of the time against
\AccCtlHigh{}\% for controls. Models that cannot say \emph{very} six times in a
row will say twelve or sixteen \emph{different} adverbs without difficulty.

This is what Assumption~\ref{ass:periodic} demands and what makes the fixed-point
account non-vacuous: only under periodic conditioning does the per-repetition map
repeat, and only then can its iterates converge.

\subsection{The states the decoder visits stop multiplying}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figs/fig2_mechanism.pdf}
\caption{(a) Effective rank of the generation trajectory against $k$, for
repeated text (solid) and length-matched controls (dashed). (b) The fitted
capacity gain $\mathrm{d}\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}}/\mathrm{d}\log k$ with 95\%
bootstrap intervals over stimulus templates.}
\label{fig:mechanism}
\end{figure*}

Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}(ii) says that under periodic conditioning the states
a decoder visits stop being mutually distinguishable. That has a direct
observable consequence: asking for more repetitions should stop buying the
decoder more distinct internal states, while asking for the same amount of
non-repetitive text should keep buying them.

We measure the number of distinguishable states as the effective rank
$\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}} = \exp(-\sum_i p_i \log p_i)$ of the generation
trajectory at deep probe layers, where $p_i$ are the normalised singular values.
The statistic is the \emph{capacity gain}
$\mathrm{d}\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}}/\mathrm{d}\log k$, fitted separately on
repeated items and on their matched controls, with intervals bootstrapped over
stimulus templates.

Figure~\ref{fig:mechanism} shows the result. On repeated text the capacity gain
is a factor \CapRatio{} of the control gain, and the two 95\% intervals are
disjoint for \NCapSepWord{} of the \NCapModels{} instrumented checkpoints. The
matched-pair form of the same comparison --- differencing each repeated item
against the control sharing its template and $k$ --- gives a positive gap in
\CapFracPos{}\% of pairs. For Llasa-1B the gains are \GainRepLlasaOneB{}
$[\GainRepLoLlasaOneB{}, \GainRepHiLlasaOneB{}]$ against
\GainCtlLlasaOneB{} $[\GainCtlLoLlasaOneB{}, \GainCtlHiLlasaOneB{}]$, with the
repeated trajectory plateauing near $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}}
= \SatRepLlasaOneB{}$ while its control climbs to \SatCtlLlasaOneB{}.

The decoder does not merely make mistakes on repeated text; it runs out of
internal states in which a mistake and a correct continuation could differ. That
is the empirical content of the theorem, measured without reference to any
behavioural outcome.

\subsection{A note on what we could not measure}
\label{sec:negative}

We first tried to measure Assumption~\ref{ass:contraction} the direct way: locate
each repetition boundary from the model's text attention and fit
$\log \lVert h_{m+1}-h_m\rVert = a + m\log q$. That estimator is unsound here and
we report it as such. Boundary localisation needs a monotone text read-head, and
the deep-layer attention centroid of these decoders advances on barely half of
generation steps, so boundary estimates collapse onto near-duplicate positions
and the resulting distances are dominated by localisation error rather than by
state dynamics. The failure is not incidental --- the flatter the attention over
repeated spans, which is exactly what Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution} predicts, the
worse any attention-based localiser becomes. The capacity measure above needs no
boundaries, which is why we adopted it.

\subsection{Attention dilutes as $1/k$}

Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution} is directly checkable in the recorded attention. Pooled
across models and deep probe layers, the median attention mass received by each
repeated occurrence scales as $k^{\AttnSlope{}}$, against the $k^{-1}$ the lemma
predicts, and text-attention entropy grows with $\log k$ at slope
\EntropySlope{}. The conditioning the decoder receives at each boundary does
become progressively less able to identify which occurrence it is rendering,
which is the empirical content of Assumption~\ref{ass:periodic}.

\subsection{Spectral signature}

Table~\ref{tab:spectral} carries over the observables of the companion ASR
study~\cite{viakhirev2026dispersion}: effective rank $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}}$,
spectral slope $\alpha$, and Kirchhoff index $Kf$ of the generation trajectory,
compared between faithful and hallucinated generations. The direction is the same
one that study found in large Whisper models under stress --- reduced effective
rank and hardened spectra --- which is what a trajectory collapsing onto a
low-dimensional attractor should look like from the outside.
